1.pericope_label: Behold, the LORD maketh the earth empty: therefore hath the curse devoured the earth, and few men left

schools.summary: Describes the genre before the content, warning that such prophecies start from circumstances which vanish like will-o'-the-wisps when pursued, and identifies the broken covenant as the universal one made with Noah rather than the national one.

Places the chapter as the summing up of everything said since the thirteenth, rejects the last-day reading as forced, and draws from the levelling of ranks an argument for the value of ordered government.
Keeps the scope national, the land of Canaan wasted by Assyrian and Chaldean in turn, and reads the equalising of buyer and seller as a common reduction to beggary and slavery.
Argues from Hebrew usage that the word must mean the earth and not one land, since a particular country is normally specified, and applies the emptiness to families and estates in any age.

debates.question: How wide is the earth that is emptied?

positions.view: the land of Canaan, wasted first by the Assyrians and then by the Chaldeans
the earth, not one country: where the word means a particular land it almost always has something joined to it saying which, and nothing does here
the wider sense predominates, since the next verse pairs the word with world
the whole survey of nations made since the thirteenth chapter, gathered into a summary; the reading that refers it to the last day is excessively forced
the papal and antichristian states, with the chapter's close reaching to the destruction of the whole world

debates.question: What is the everlasting covenant that has been broken?

positions.view: the covenant made with Noah, so that the charge is universal rather than national, the verb for defiled covering every sin that desecrates humanity
the law, which the versions read in the singular
three distinct charges: transgressing revelations, setting the ordinance at nought, breaking the everlasting covenant

outliers.reading: Alone reasons backwards from the curse to a doctrine of civil order: since the loss of all distinction between people and priest is reckoned among God's judgments, ordered government must be pleasing to him, for when it is taken away the life of man differs little from the sustenance of cattle and beasts of prey.

Alone characterises the whole cycle of four chapters, warning that its apparently sharp historical circumstances vanish like will-o'-the-wisps when followed, and refusing the genuineness test that modern critics have applied to it.

themes: Behold, the Lord maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof.

And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him.
The land shall be utterly emptied, and utterly spoiled: for the Lord hath spoken this word.
The earth mourneth and fadeth away, the world languisheth and fadeth away, the haughty people of the earth do languish.
The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant.
Therefore hath the curse devoured the earth, and they that dwell therein are desolate: therefore the inhabitants of the earth are burned, and few men left.

7.pericope_label: The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth: in the city is left desolation, and the gate is smitten with destruction

schools.summary: Renders the ruined city as the city of chaos, the world cast back out of its cosmos into the formlessness it began in, and defends the received text where others would emend it.
Reads the failed vintage as an indictment of luxury without condemning wine itself, and names the cause of the city's fall as the banishment of justice and good government from it.
Explains the grief of senseless things as a figure usual in all authors, identifies the strong drink as palm wine, and proposes two textual changes in as many verses.
Turns to the remnant in the middle of the wrath, and finds in the gleanings of an olive tree both their fewness and their concealment.

positions.view: the city of chaos: the world thrown back out of its cosmos into its primeval formlessness, its houses shut not by barred gates but by their own ruins
chiefly Jerusalem, though it reaches other cities; named from its crimes rather than its punishment, since justice and good government have been banished from it
Jerusalem and other cities, the singular taken collectively, a city of disorder breaking all the laws God had established
mystical Babylon, that is, Rome, devoted to ruin and desolation

debates.question: Should the darkening of joy be emended?

positions.view: yes: transpose a letter and read that gladness has passed away
no: the English verb exactly expresses a Hebrew word used of the gloom of sunset, the light of joy passing into the blackness of darkness

outliers.reading: Alone guards the passage from proving too much, insisting that to drink wine is not in itself evil since God appointed it for man's use, and that what is condemned is the banquet of drunkards and the want men bring on themselves by turning his goodness to bad use.

Alone works the olive-gleaning figure for two properties of the remnant, that they are dispersed and at a distance from one another and that they are concealed under the leaves, so that the Lord knows those who are his though the world does not.

themes: The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth, all the merryhearted do sigh.
The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth.
They shall not drink wine with a song; strong drink shall be bitter to them that drink it.
The city of confusion is broken down: every house is shut up, that no man may come in.
There is a crying for wine in the streets; all joy is darkened, the mirth of the land is gone.
In the city is left desolation, and the gate is smitten with destruction.
When thus it shall be in the midst of the land among the people, there shall be as the shaking of an olive tree, and as the gleaning grapes when the vintage is done.

14.pericope_label: They shall lift up their voice, they shall sing for the majesty of the LORD: but I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me

schools.summary: Reads the disputed word as the east set against the isles as the west, denies that the righteous one can be a name for God, and describes the church refined by judgment and called to the whole world.
Takes the same word for hidden valleys and makes their isolation the point, that no corner will be too obscure for God's praises, and marks the two halves of the verse as apparently at variance.
Prefers to emend the word to isles on the strength of the following clause, and takes the fires as the furnace of affliction and the treachery as that of the prophet's own people.
Finds the comfort in the geography, that saints driven to the ends of the earth are heard singing rather than sighing, and keeps the righteous one as the righteous God.

debates.question: What does the disputed word in the summons to glorify mean?

positions.view: the fires of affliction, though the word has the form of the high priest's Urim and has also been rendered doctrines, valleys, and the clefts where the persecuted hid
isles, by emendation, justified by the repetition of the word in the next clause with the sea added
the east, taken as light and set against the isles of the sea as the west, giving the familiar span from sunrise to sunset and the more vivid antithesis
hidden valleys, shut in by mountains and so cut off, whose inhabitants converse less with others; the sense being that no corner is too obscure for God's praise to reach
the furnace of affliction

debates.question: Who is the righteous one glorified in the song?

positions.view: not God: he is never so called in this absolute way, so the phrase means the church of righteous men
not God, on two grounds: the word is honour rather than the term used in doxologies, and the title is never used absolutely of him; render it honour to the righteous, the true Israel
the righteous God, the word being singular, who is just in all he has brought upon us
the Lord, the righteous one

outliers.reading: Alone reports an Aramaic sense that turns the cry of leanness into a cry about a secret, and remarks on the strange succession of uncouth sounds the Hebrew makes at this point.

Alone draws a social observation from the geography of the valleys, that countries shut in by mountains are separated by nature and their people less civilised for having fewer opportunities of conversing with each other.

themes: They shall lift up their voice, they shall sing for the majesty of the Lord, they shall cry aloud from the sea.
Wherefore glorify ye the Lord in the fires, even the name of the Lord God of Israel in the isles of the sea.

From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous. But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me! the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously.

17.pericope_label: Fear, and the pit, and the snare, are upon thee: the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and before his ancients gloriously

schools.summary: Hears the threefold naming of the earth as the three stages of an earthquake and the rhythm as an echo of the crashes, renders the shelter a hammock swinging in the wind, and carries the punishment up to the powers in heavenly places.

Refuses to take the reeling physically and refers it to the collapse of government, and argues from the weight of iniquity that God is never angry without cause, since we are the authors of the evils we suffer.
Reconstructs the ancient hunting apparatus behind the three words of the threat, and reads the high ones as the ecclesiastical and civil polity of the nation.

debates.question: Who are the host of the high ones that are on high?

positions.view: the principalities and powers in heavenly places, perhaps the gods the nations worshipped; the parallelism of the two clauses is decisive against reading them as merely earthly
the ecclesiastical and civil polity of the nation, which shall be destroyed

neither the stars nor the devils nor the Jews, all of which readings must be refused: the sense is that no power is high enough to escape, since though they rise above the clouds God's hand reaches them
both together: if the old earth passes out of the system of the universe, punishment falls at once on the princes of heaven and the princes of earth

debates.question: What is the shelter the earth is likened to?

positions.view: a hammock, a hanging mat slung from a tree in which the vineyard keeper slept, moving with every breath of wind and so the very type of instability
a lodge for a night
not a figure of the earth at all: no change is meant in its position, and the words refer to men, meaning that no kingly power or regular government would be left

outliers.reading: Alone reconstructs the hunt behind the three words: the terror a line strung with coloured feathers that fluttered and drove the beasts into the toils, the pit dug deep and covered with boughs and turf, the snare a series of nets thrown round a wide space and drawn in by degrees.

Alone hears the threefold naming of the earth as a climax representing the three stages of an earthquake, the first cleavage, the wide gaping and the final shattering, with the rhythm of the passage almost an echo of the crashes.

themes: Fear, and the pit, and the snare, are upon thee, O inhabitant of the earth.

And it shall come to pass, that he who fleeth from the noise of the fear shall fall into the pit; and he that cometh up out of the midst of the pit shall be taken in the snare: for the windows from on high are open, and the foundations of the earth do shake.
The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly.
The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again.
And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall punish the host of the high ones that are on high, and the kings of the earth upon the earth.
And they shall be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison, and after many days shall they be visited.
Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously.
